Signature: `/brakeTransitionDuration (int)motorID (int)duration`.

Arguments:

- `motorID` (int, range 1-4 (STEP400), 1-8 (STEP800)): Motor ID
- `duration` (int, range 0-65535 ms): Transitional duration

#### /brakeStatus

Signature: `/brakeStatus (int)motorID (int)state`. Added in v2.2.0.

Arguments:

- `motorID` (int, range 1-4 (STEP400), 1-8 (STEP800)): Motor ID
- `state` (int): State of the brake
  - `-1`: The electromagnetic brake is disabled for the motor
  - `0`: Engaged. Brake output: engaged. Driver: HiZ
  - `1`: Releasing (`/activate 1`, waiting `brakeTransitionDuration`). Brake output: engaged. Driver: energized
  - `2`: Released. Brake output: released. Driver: energized
  - `3`: Stopping (`/softHiZ`, `/activate 0`: decelerating, engages when stopped). Brake output: released. Driver: energized
  - `4`: Engaging (waiting `brakeTransitionDuration`, then HiZ). Brake output: engaged. Driver: energized
  - `5`: Free (`/free`). Brake output: released. Driver: HiZ

Description:

Reply to `/getBrakeStatus`. The state numbers are part of the specification; new states will only be added as 6, 7, ....

#### /servoParam

Signature: `/servoParam (int)motorID (float)kP (float)kI (float)kD`.

Arguments:

- `motorID` (int, range 1-4 (STEP400), 1-8 (STEP800)): Motor ID
- `kP` (float): Proportional control gain
- `kI` (float): Integral control gain
- `kD` (float): Differential control gain

#### /booted

Signature: `/booted (int)deviceID (int)resetCause`.

Arguments:

- `deviceID` (int, range 0-255): The device ID set by the DIP Switch
- `resetCause` (int): The cause of the reset, as reported by the MCU. Added in v2.2.0.
  - `0`: Unknown
  - `1`: Power-on. Treat 1 and 2 both as a reset by the power supply
  - `2`: Brown-out (supply voltage drop). On the SAMD21 a normal power-up is often reported as 2
  - `3`: Reset pin
  - `4`: Watchdog
  - `5`: Software reset (for example after `/resetDevice` or a firmware upload over USB)
  - `6`: CPU fault: the reset after a CPU exception (HardFault on the SAMD21)

Description:

This message is automatically sent out when the device has (re)started. By watching the message, you can detect reset event of the device triggered by some reason.

The message will be sent out one second after the firmware is started up and the ethernet link is established. The message will be sent to `255.255.255.255`, means broadcasting to all nodes within the subnet.

This message can be disabled from the browser configuration tool.

`resetCause`: the numbers are part of the specification; new causes will only be added as 7, 8, .... A client should treat a number it does not know as "other", and accept 6. If several causes are flagged, the first of CPU fault, brown-out, power-on, watchdog, reset pin, software is reported. After a power-on or a brown-out the CPU fault is never reported, so a fault followed by a power cycle reports 1 or 2. The numbers are those reported by the MCU as they are; with another MCU in the future the same operation may report a different number (the meaning of each number does not change).

Changes:

- v2.2.0: A second argument, `resetCause` (`i`), is added: `/booted myId resetCause`. Clients that check the exact number of arguments are affected.
- v2.2.0: After a watchdog detects a hang (about 250 ms after the last watchdog reset), every brake output is engaged first and the firmware waits for the longest `brakeTransitionDuration` of the motors with the brake enabled and not engaged (at most 1 s) before the board is reset, so the reset comes up to 1 s later than before; `resetCause` is still 4. v2.1.0 reset the board about 62.5 ms after a hang.
- v2.2.0: A CPU fault (HardFault) now engages every brake output at once, waits as above (at most 1 s), and restarts with `resetCause` 6.
- v2.2.0: The reset by `/resetDevice` now reports `resetCause` 5 (software).

#### /error/osc

Signature: `/error/osc (string)errorText`.

Arguments:

- `errorText` (string): A character string that indicates the details of an error.
  - `MessageNotMatch`: There is no corresponding command
  - `OscSyntaxError`: The OSC format is out of standard. Also sent for a packet larger than 512 bytes and for a message with more than 16 arguments. **v2.2.0**: Also sent for a packet larger than 512 bytes and for a message with more than 16 arguments.
  - `WrongDataType`: Wrong datatype of in argument(s): a string for a number, NaN or infinity, or a non-string for `/setConfigName`. Nothing is applied. **v2.2.0**: Nothing is applied. Before, such an argument was applied as 0.
  - `MissingArgument`: The message has fewer arguments than the command needs. Nothing is applied. Added in v2.2.0.

Description:

Sent if any error is detected in the received OSC (Open Sound Control) message.

The arguments of every command are checked before the command is applied. Arguments beyond the ones a command needs are ignored. The message is not sent while error reports are disabled (`/reportError`).

Changes:

- v2.2.0: `MissingArgument` is new: a command with too few arguments replies it and applies nothing. Before, missing arguments were applied as 0 (`/setKval 1` set every KVAL of motor 1 to 0, `/setSpeedProfile 1` set acc, dec and max speed to 0, and the positions missing in `/setTargetPositionList` became 0).
- v2.2.0: `WrongDataType` is replied for an argument of the wrong type (a string for a number, NaN or infinity, `/setConfigName` with a non-string) and applies nothing. Before, the argument was applied as 0.
- v2.2.0: A packet larger than 512 bytes and a message with more than 16 arguments are answered with `OscSyntaxError`.
- v2.2.0: In some corner cases where the former OSC library read past the end of the address pattern (for example characters following a `{...}` list), the match result can differ from before.

#### /error/command

Signature: `/error/command (string)errorText (int)motorID`.

Arguments:

- `errorText` (string): A character string that indicates the details of an error.
  - `CommandIgnored`: The command is currently not executable. Also refer Timing section. Also sent when a value is outside the range of the command; nothing is applied (the motor ID is 255 for `/setPositionListReportInterval`).
  - `MotorIdNotMatch`: Motor ID is not appropriate. A motor ID outside 0-255 is replied with the value sent. **v2.2.0**: A motor ID outside 0-255 is replied with the value sent. Before, 257 and 511 were read as 1 and 255.
  - `BrakeEngaged`: A motion command was sent while the electromagnetic brake was active. Also sent for `/enableServoMode 1` and `/homing` while the brake is engaged, releasing or engaging (not while stopping or after `/free`).
  - `HomeSwActivating`: Movement from home switch position towards the origin point. Also sent by `/goUntil` and `/goUntilRaw` when the home switch is already activated. **v2.2.0**: Sent by `/goUntil` and `/goUntilRaw` when the home switch is already activated. It was sent as `HomeSwActivated` before.
  - `LimitSwActivating`: Movement from limit switch position towards the opposite direction from origin. Available on STEP400 only.
  - `GoUntilTimeout`: Timeout while executing `/goUntil` command.
  - `ReleaseSwTimeout`: Timeout while executing `/releaseSw` command.
  - `InServoMode`: Received a command which can not be executed while servo mode. **v2.2.0**: Also sent for `/goUntil`, `/goUntilRaw` and `/releaseSw`.
  - `BrakeReleaseFailed`: `/activate 1` was sent but the driver stayed HiZ (for example without motor power), so the brake stays engaged. Added in v2.2.0.
  - `BrakeEngagedOnHiZ`: The driver went HiZ by itself (overcurrent shutdown, thermal shutdown, UVLO) while the brake was released, so the brake was engaged. Added in v2.2.0.
  - `ServoModeCancelledOnHiZ`: The driver went HiZ by itself (overcurrent shutdown, thermal shutdown, UVLO) in the servo mode, so the servo mode was cancelled. Enable it again with `/enableServoMode 1`. Added in v2.2.0.
  - `MotorNotHiZ`: The command writes a driver register that can be written only while the outputs are HiZ, and the motor is not HiZ. A motor holding its position is not HiZ: send `/softHiZ` or `/hardHiZ` first. Nothing is applied. Added in v2.2.0.
  - `MotorNotStopped`: The command writes a driver register that can be written only while the motor is stopped or HiZ, and the motor is turning. Nothing is applied. Added in v2.2.0.
- `motorID` (int, range 1-4 (STEP400), 1-8 (STEP800)): The motor's ID

Description:

This message will be sent if an error is detected while executing a command.
The message can be enabled or disabled with `/reportError` command.

With 255 (all motors), each motor is judged alone for the errors that depend on the state of a motor (`MotorNotHiZ`, `MotorNotStopped`): the motors in the required state are changed and the others reply the error.

Changes:

- v2.2.0: New errors: `BrakeReleaseFailed`, `BrakeEngagedOnHiZ`, `ServoModeCancelledOnHiZ` (electromagnetic brake and servo mode), `MotorNotHiZ` and `MotorNotStopped` (registers that can be written only in some states). All follow `/reportError`.
- v2.2.0: `CommandIgnored` is also replied when a value is outside the range of the command, and nothing is applied: `/setPositionReportInterval` and `/setPositionListReportInterval` above 65535 (255 for the list), `/setGoUntilTimeout` and `/setReleaseSwTimeout` below 0, `/setElPos` with a full step outside 0-3 or a microstep outside 0-127, `/setServoParam` with a negative gain, `/setBrakeTransitionDuration` outside 0-65535, `/setDecayModeParam` with TON_MIN or TOFF_MIN above 127.
- v2.2.0: `MotorIdNotMatch` is replied for a motor ID outside 0-255, with the value sent. Before, 257 and 511 were read as 1 and 255.
- v2.2.0: `HomeSwActivating` is replied by `/goUntil` and `/goUntilRaw` for an activated home switch. It was sent as `HomeSwActivated`, and it now follows `/reportError` like the other command errors.

## Configuration file

Items of the configuration file (JSON on the microSD card). The initial value is the one used when the file or the key is missing.

### information

- `information.configName` (Configuration name): string, initial value Default (firmware) / "" (template).
  Configuration file name. Can be set freely.
  Commands: `/setConfigName`.
- `information.configVersion` (Configuration version): version, initial value 0.0 (firmware) / 1.2 (template).
  Version of the configuration file format. A `.json` file without it is not accepted (`config.txt` is accepted without it). Unable to modify.
- `information.targetProduct` (Target product): string, initial value STEP400: --- (firmware) / STEP400 (template); STEP800: --- (firmware) / STEP800 (template).
  Name of the target product for the config file. Unable to modify.

### network

- `network.myIp` (My IP address): ip, initial value 10.0.0.100.
  Set the IP address. if `ID adds to my IP` is checked, ID value added to this address becomes the actual IP address. For example if the IP address is set to `10.0.0.100` and ID switch is set to 1, `10.0.0.101` will be the actual address. Be cautious not the added value to exceed 254.
- `network.isMyIpAddId` (ID adds to my IP): bool, initial value true.
  If the address with the ID added would be beyond .254 (ID 155 or more with the default 10.0.0.100), the ID is not added: the configured address is used and a warning is printed on USB serial.
- `network.destIp` (Destination IP): ip, initial value 10.0.0.10.
  Commands: `/setDestIp`.
- `network.dns` (DNS): ip, initial value 10.0.0.1.
- `network.gateway` (Gateway): ip, initial value 10.0.0.1.
- `network.subnet` (Subnet mask): ip, initial value 255.255.255.0.
- `network.inPort` (Incoming port): int, initial value 50000.
  The port number that the device receives OSC messages.
- `network.outPort` (Outgoing port): int, initial value 50100.
  The port number that the device send out OSC message. If `ID adds to Outgoing port` check box is checked, the ID value will be added to the port number.
- `network.isOutPortAddId` (ID adds to Outgoing port): bool, initial value true.
  If the port with the ID added would be beyond 65535, the ID is not added: the configured port is used and a warning is printed on USB serial.
- `network.mac` (MAC address): mac, initial value STEP400: 60:95:CE:10:06:00 (firmware) / 60:95:CE:10:02:00 (template); STEP800: 60:95:CE:10:06:00 (firmware) / 60:95:CE:10:03:00 (template).
  You can switch decimal and hexadecimal display by clicking the check box `Hex`.
- `network.isMacAddId` (ID adds to MAC address): bool, initial value true.
  When this check box is checked, the ID value will be added to the lowest byte of the MAC address.
- `network.bootedMsgEnable` (Booted message enable): bool, initial value true.
  Enables or disables the auto message `/booted` on ethernet link establishment on start.
- `network.canSendMsgBeforeDestIp` (Allow OSC reply before /setDestIp): bool, initial value false.
  In initial state, the controller does not send OSC response until receiving `/setDestIp`. However if this check box is checked, the controller will sends out OSC message immediately after boot up. Known issue in v2.2.0: the running board keeps "`/setDestIp` has been received" in the same value as this setting. After `/setDestIp` was received, saving the configuration (`/saveConfig`, or saving with the browser configuration tool) writes `true` to the card. When the browser configuration tool writes `false`, the running value also becomes `false`, and the board sends no reply until `/setDestIp` is sent again. Workaround: send `/setDestIp` again after saving, and check the value in the saved file.
- `network.reportError` (Report errors): bool, initial value true.
  Commands: `/reportError`.

### alarmAndReport

- `alarmAndReport.reportBUSY` (Report BUSY): bool, initial value false, per motor.
  Commands: `/enableBusyReport`.
- `alarmAndReport.reportHiZ` (Report HiZ): bool, initial value false, per motor.
  Commands: `/enableHizReport`.
- `alarmAndReport.reportHomeSwStatus` (Report HOME switch status): bool, initial value false, per motor.
  Commands: `/enableHomeSwReport`.
- `alarmAndReport.reportLimitSwStatus` (Report LIMIT switch status): bool, initial value false, per motor.
  Available on STEP400 only.
  Commands: `/enableLimitSwReport`.
- `alarmAndReport.reportDir` (Report motor direction): bool, initial value false, per motor.
  Commands: `/enableDirReport`.
- `alarmAndReport.reportMotorStatus` (Report Motor Status): bool, initial value false, per motor.
  Commands: `/enableMotorStatusReport`.
- `alarmAndReport.reportSwEvn` (Report HOME switch event): bool, initial value false, per motor.
  Commands: `/enableSwEventReport`.
- `alarmAndReport.reportUVLO` (Report undervoltage lockout): bool, initial value true, per motor.
  Commands: `/enableUvloReport`.
- `alarmAndReport.reportThermalStatus` (Report thermal status of driver chip): bool, initial value true, per motor.
  Commands: `/enableThermalStatusReport`.
- `alarmAndReport.reportOCD` (Report overcurrent detection): bool, initial value true, per motor.
  Commands: `/enableOverCurrentReport`.
- `alarmAndReport.reportStall` (Report motor stall detection): bool, initial value false, per motor.
  Stall detection lets the driver detect, from the motor current, that the motor can no longer turn against the load. Find a threshold (`/setStallThreshold`) as close as possible to, and slightly above, the current actually flowing. A small loss of steps cannot be detected, but a large position error may be.
  Commands: `/enableStallReport`.
- `alarmAndReport.reportPositionInterval` (Report position interval): int, range 0-65535 ms, initial value 0, per motor.
  The interval of the position report (`/position`) of each motor. 0 turns the report off. The value is not range-checked when the configuration file is read (or written over USB serial). An out-of-range value wraps around: the value after the maximum is 0 (65536 becomes 0, which turns the report off; 65537 becomes 1; -1 becomes 65535). `/setPositionReportInterval` rejects a value above 65535 with `CommandIgnored`, and a negative value turns the report off.
  Commands: `/setPositionReportInterval`.
- `alarmAndReport.reportPositionListInterval` (Report position list interval): int, range 0-65535 ms, initial value 0.
  The interval of the position list report (`/positionList`). 0 turns the report off. When it is greater than 0, the position report of each motor (`/position`) is turned off. The value is not range-checked when the configuration file is read (or written over USB serial). An out-of-range value wraps around: the value after the maximum is 0 (65536 becomes 0, 65537 becomes 1, and -1 becomes 65535). `/setPositionListReportInterval` rejects a value above 65535 with `CommandIgnored`.
  Commands: `/setPositionListReportInterval`.
- `alarmAndReport.OCThreshold` (Overcurrent threshold): int, initial value STEP400: 15 (5A); STEP800: 7 (3A), per motor.
  Commands: `/setOverCurrentThreshold`.

### driverSettings

- `driverSettings.homingAtStartup` (Homing when the system starts): bool, initial value false, per motor.
  Proceed to homing movement soon after boot when this check box is checked. With the electromagnetic brake enabled, the brake is released first, as `/activate` does, and the homing starts once the brake is released. **v2.2.0**: With the electromagnetic brake enabled, the brake is released first, as `/activate 1` does, and the homing starts once the brake is released. Before, the homing failed because the brake was engaged, and the timeout of the homing later sent a hard stop to the HiZ motor.
- `driverSettings.homingDirection` (Homing Direction): int, range 1: Forward, 0: Reverse, initial value 0 (Reverse), per motor.
  Commands: `/setHomingDirection`.
- `driverSettings.homingSpeed` (Homing Speed): float, range step/s, initial value 50, per motor.
  Commands: `/setHomingSpeed`.
- `driverSettings.homeSwMode` (Home switch won't cause HardStop): bool, initial value true, per motor.
  Commands: `/setHomeSwMode`.
- `driverSettings.prohibitMotionOnHomeSw` (Prohibit motions on HomeSw): bool, initial value false, per motor.
  Commands: `/setProhibitMotionOnHomeSw`.
- `driverSettings.limitSwMode` (Limit switch won't cause HardStop): bool, initial value true, per motor.
  Available on STEP400 only.
  Commands: `/setLimitSwMode`.
- `driverSettings.prohibitMotionOnLimitSw` (Prohibit motions on LimitSw): bool, initial value false, per motor.
  Available on STEP400 only.
  Commands: `/setProhibitMotionOnLimitSw`.
- `driverSettings.goUntilTimeout` (goUntil timeout duration): int, range ms, initial value 10000, per motor.
  Commands: `/setGoUntilTimeout`.
- `driverSettings.releaseSwTimeout` (releaseSw timeout duration): int, range ms, initial value 10000, per motor.
  Commands: `/setReleaseSwTimeout`.
- `driverSettings.stepMode` (Microstepping mode): int, initial value 7, per motor.
  Commands: `/setMicrostepMode`.
- `driverSettings.isCurrentMode` (Current mode): bool, initial value false, per motor.
  Available on STEP400 only.
  Commands: `/setVoltageMode`, `/setCurrentMode`.
- `driverSettings.slewRate` (Slew rate): int, range 0-5 (STEP400), 0-2 (STEP800); STEP400: 0: 114V/us, 1: 220V/us, 2: 400V/us, 3: 520V/us, 4: 790V/us, 5: 980V/us; STEP800: 0: 180V/us, 1: 290V/us, 2: 530V/us, initial value STEP400: 5 (980V/us); STEP800: 2 (530V/us), per motor.
  Set the slew rate (steepness of rising) of motor control current from a motor driver in 6 steps for STEP400, 3 steps for STEP800. A value outside the range in the configuration file is not rejected: it is limited to the range (a negative value becomes 0, a larger one the highest value).
- `driverSettings.electromagnetBrakeEnable` (Electromagnetic brake enable): bool, initial value false, per motor.
  Commands: `/enableElectromagnetBrake`.
- `driverSettings.brakeTransitionDuration` (Brake transition duration): int, range 0-65535 ms, initial value 100, per motor.
  The time to wait for the brake to release or to engage. See `/setBrakeTransitionDuration`. The value is not range-checked when the configuration file is read (or written over USB serial). An out-of-range value wraps around: the value after the maximum is 0 (65536 becomes 0, 65537 becomes 1, and -1 becomes 65535). `/setBrakeTransitionDuration` rejects such a value with `CommandIgnored`.
  Commands: `/setBrakeTransitionDuration`.

### speedProfile

## Functional guides

### Functional guides

The functional guides explain how each function of the STEP Series works: the concepts, the states and how they change, and which commands to use in which order. They describe what happens and why. The arguments, the ranges and the replies of each command are in the OSC reference, which the guides link to.

#### Guides

- Communication and messages: how the board sends and receives OSC messages, `/setDestIp`, replies and automatically sent messages, and the errors of the arguments.
- Voltage mode and current mode: the two ways of driving the motor, KVAL and TVAL, and how to switch between them.
- Speed profile and types of motor motion: acceleration, deceleration and maximum speed; constant speed, positioning and the four kinds of stop.
- Homing and position management: finding the reference position with the HOME and LIMIT switches, and the collision prevention settings.
- Servo mode: following a target position that changes in real time, and how to tune the PID gains.
- Electromagnetic brake: the states of the brake, how each command acts on it, and what to keep in mind for a hanging load.
- Alarms and protection: undervoltage lockout, overtemperature, overcurrent and stall, and how the board reports them.

For the connections and the settings, see Connections and settings.

### Communication and messages

This page explains how the board exchanges OSC (Open Sound Control) messages with your computer: how it learns where to send them, what it sends by itself, and what it does with the arguments it receives.

#### Overview

The board receives OSC messages as UDP packets. It sends two kinds of messages back: the **replies** to the commands that ask for something (such as `/getVersion`), and the messages that it sends **by itself** when something happens or at a fixed interval (such as `/busy` or `/position`). Both go to the **destination**, the IP address and port that the board keeps for this purpose.

For how to set the IP address of the board, the port numbers and the DIP switch, see Network and the DIP switch. They are not repeated here.

#### The destination and `/setDestIp`

##### When to send `/setDestIp`

The board does not know where to send messages until it receives `/setDestIp`: it takes the sender of this message as the destination. Until then it sends nothing, except the broadcast `/booted`. (With `network.canSendMsgBeforeDestIp` set, the board sends to `network.destIp` from the start.)

Send `/setDestIp`:

- at the start of the connection, and
- when the network or the computer changes: another computer or network adapter with the same IP address, or a switch between Wi-Fi and wired. When you replace the computer, wait at least 1.5 s after the last message that the old one sent.

Without it, the board keeps sending to the MAC address of the old computer. Your commands still work, but no reply and no report reaches you. (When the computer is connected directly and the link goes down and up again, the board recovers by itself; through a switch it does not.)

##### Resolving the MAC address

When the destination is set (or changes) by a `/setDestIp` that is from a new address, or comes 1.5 s or more after the last packet from the destination (a `/setDestIp` sent every second as a heartbeat does not start it), the board has to find the MAC address of the destination. It sends one byte of UDP to port 9 (discard) of the broadcast address, then one byte to port 9 of the destination at once and every 150 ms, until the destination answers the ARP request or a few seconds have passed. The computer may answer each of these packets with an ICMP port unreachable message, which is harmless; it can show up in the log of a firewall.

The reply `/destIp` of the `/setDestIp` that starts this resolution is sent when the resolution is done. On a wired network it comes a few ms after the command; **when the computer is on Wi-Fi it can take up to a few seconds**. If `/destIp` does not come, send `/setDestIp` again.

While the MAC address is being resolved (after such a `/setDestIp`, and after the link comes up again; also after the board starts, when it sends before `/setDestIp`), the messages to the destination are **dropped**, not sent later: no replies and no reports arrive. The broadcast `/booted` is still sent.

While the board waits for a destination that does not answer the ARP request, it cannot process OSC messages: each probe that fails stops the processing for up to about 41 ms, and the probes come every 150 ms. A wired computer answers the first probe at once; a computer on Wi-Fi often needs several, so the processing stops repeatedly during the resolution. This disturbs the monitoring of the electromagnetic brake and the servo mode. **We recommend that you send `/setDestIp` while the motors are stopped.**

A send to a destination that has never answered ARP (for example a wrong destination address) fails. The board then pauses all the sends to that destination for 1 s and drops the messages in that time; after that it tries again with the next message. A packet that arrives from the destination resumes the sends at once.

##### Checking the connection

To check that the board is alive, send a command that has a reply, such as `/getVersion`. Do not use `/setDestIp` for this.

#### Replies and messages that the board sends by itself

- **Replies.** A command that asks for a value (`/get...`) is answered with a message, and so are some set commands. What a command returns is written in its reference.
- **Notifications of changes.** The board reads the state of the drivers every 5 ms and sends a message when the state changes: `/busy`, `/HiZ`, `/dir`, `/motorStatus`, `/homeSw`, `/limitSw`, `/swEvent`, `/uvlo`, `/thermalStatus`, `/overCurrent`, `/stall` and so on. Each of them is turned on and off with its own `/enable...Report` command, and the settings of the board decide which of them are on at the start. A state is sent only when it changes. For the alarms see Alarms and protection.
- **Reports at a fixed interval.** `/setPositionReportInterval` makes the board send `/position` of a motor at an interval, and `/setPositionListReportInterval` makes it send the positions of all the motors in a single message, `/positionList`. To get the positions of all the motors at short intervals, use the list report: it needs much less of the CPU of the board than one report per motor.
- **`/booted`** is broadcast when the board starts. It contains the reason of the reset.

The full list is in Automatically sent messages.

#### The arguments that the board receives

The board checks the arguments of a command before it applies the command. When a check fails, **nothing is applied**.

| Case | Error |
| --- | --- |
| Fewer arguments than the command needs | `/error/osc` `MissingArgument` |
| An argument of the wrong type (a string where a number is needed, NaN or infinity, or a non-string for `/setConfigName`) | `/error/osc` `WrongDataType` |
| A motor ID that the board does not have (not a motor of the board, and not 255), or outside 0-255 | `/error/command` `MotorIdNotMatch`, with the motor ID that was sent |
| A value outside the range of the command | `/error/command` `CommandIgnored` |
| A packet larger than 512 bytes, or more than 16 arguments | `/error/osc` `OscSyntaxError` |

Before v2.2.0, missing arguments and arguments of the wrong type were applied as 0. For example `/setKval 1` set every KVAL of the motor to 0.

- Arguments beyond the ones that a command needs are ignored.
- Some commands do not reject a value outside the range but limit it or wrap it around. The reference of each command says which; see also the Common rules: Messages to the board.
- An integer and a floating-point number are converted into each other. **Send a logical value as the integer 0 or 1** (type tag `i`); that is how the STEP Series defines it, and the board always sends logical values this way. The board also accepts a number (an integer greater than 0, or a float of 1.0 or more, is true) and the OSC values True and False.
- OSC bundles are not supported.

#### Errors

Two messages report errors:

- `/error/osc`: the message itself could not be used: a missing argument, a wrong type, a syntax error, or an address that the board does not know (`MessageNotMatch`).
- `/error/command`: the message was understood, but the command could not be executed or was not applied: the state of the motor does not allow it (`MotorNotHiZ`, `BrakeEngaged`, `InServoMode`, ...), a value was out of the range, a motor ID did not exist, a timeout elapsed.

With `/reportError` set to 0, the board sends neither of them. The list of the errors is in Automatically sent messages, and the errors of a command are listed in its reference.

#### Diagnosis

The USB serial port shows the MAC address of the destination and more about the connection. See Diagnosis via USB serial port.

#### Related commands and settings

Related commands: see the section OSC commands.

Related configuration items: see the section Configuration file.

### Voltage mode and current mode

A stepper motor can be driven with a constant voltage (voltage mode) or with a constant current (current mode). This page explains how the two differ, what KVAL and TVAL are, and how to switch between the modes.

#### The difference between voltage control and current control

There are two types of stepping control methods: constant voltage control (**voltage mode**) and constant current control (**current mode**). Only the STEP400 can switch between voltage mode and current mode; the STEP800 works in voltage mode only. The commands for the current mode, such as `/setCurrentMode` and `/setTval`, do not exist on the STEP800; see Differences between STEP400 and STEP800. The difference between the modes is explained well in this presentation PDF by STMicroelectronics.

In short:

- Voltage mode is quiet and smooth, but it can run only at lower speeds.
- Current mode is noisy, but it can reach higher speeds.

##### Test with the STEP400

A demonstration video of the test: Voltage mode and current mode test (Vimeo)

We tested both modes with a STEP400 and a motor with a microphone attached to its body, so that the smallest noises were captured. In voltage mode the motor ran quietly, but from around 800 steps/s it began to vibrate and it stalled at about 1,400 steps/s. In current mode the motor was noisy, but it ran faster than 11,000 steps/s before it began to vibrate and stalled.

#### KVAL and TVAL

The **KVAL** registers control the drive voltage in voltage mode, and the **TVAL** registers control the drive current in current mode. Both act as multipliers: KVAL sets what fraction of the supply voltage is applied to the motor, and TVAL sets the target current. Inside the driver they are the same registers, but the firmware keeps the two sets of values separate and rewrites the registers when the mode is changed, so that a value for one mode is never used by accident in the other.

Each of them has four values, for holding, running, accelerating and decelerating. `/setKval` and `/setTval` set all four at once, and `/setHoldKval`, `/setRunKval` and so on set one. `/getKval`, `/getTval` and `/getTval_mA` return the settings that were made, not the registers (in voltage mode the TVAL registers are not written, and in current mode the KVAL registers are not).

When the motor has an electromagnetic brake, the holding value is raised automatically. See Electromagnetic brake.

#### Voltage mode setting

In voltage mode, KVAL sets the percentage of the supply voltage that is applied to the motor. If a high-voltage power source is used, excessive current may flow when the motor is turning at low speed. To compensate for this, there is a group of registers (the back-EMF compensation) that lowers the applied voltage at low speed and raises it at high speed. They are set with `/setBemfParam` or with the browser configuration tool.

How to calculate the register values is described in the STMicroelectronics application note AN4144. For some motors we calculated the values from the datasheet and from measurements; they are in Example parameter values for example steppers. There are only a few of them at the moment, and we plan to add more. If you have a motor that is not listed and you have determined the values yourself, we would be glad if you shared them with us and the community.

The values depend on the supply voltage. A set of values that suits one voltage can be too strong at another one: the default back-EMF compensation was too strong at 24 V. When you change the power supply, check the values again.

#### Current mode setting

In current mode, which is available on the STEP400 only, the TVAL registers set the target current. The current of a TVAL value is

> current = (TVAL + 1) × 78.125 mA

so the value 0 is 78.125 mA, not 0 A. The STEP400 limits TVAL to a maximum of about 5 A even though the PowerSTEP01 can drive up to 10 A, because of the power rating of the current-sensing resistor of the board. A value above the limit is limited to it, not rejected. The values and the currents are listed in `/setTval`. The thresholds of overcurrent and stall use the same kind of conversion; see Alarms and protection.

A high-voltage power supply is needed to deliver the target current when the motor runs at high speed. At a phase current of 5 A the torque is very strong, and the tiniest mistake can lead to great physical danger. In such situations we recommend using an industrial-grade motor driver.

#### Switching between the modes

Use these commands to switch between the modes:

- `/setVoltageMode`: switch to voltage mode.
- `/setCurrentMode`: switch to current mode.

The outputs of the motor must be HiZ before the mode is switched. A motor that is holding its position is not HiZ. For example, to switch motor 1 to current mode, send these commands in this order:

1. `/hardHiZ 1`
2. `/setCurrentMode 1`

If the motor is not HiZ, the board replies `/error/command MotorNotHiZ` and does not change the mode (see Command executable timing in the common rules).

Current mode supports microsteps only up to 1/16. When the motor is switched to current mode with a finer microstep setting, the microstep setting becomes 1/16, and `/setMicrostepMode` replies `CommandIgnored` for a finer setting while the motor is in current mode. When the microstep setting changes, the coordinate system changes too: one rotation of a 200-step motor is 200 × 128 = 25600 steps in 1/128 microstep mode, but 200 × 16 = 3200 steps in 1/16 microstep mode.

#### Related commands and settings

Related commands: see the section OSC commands.

Related configuration items: see the section Configuration file.

### Speed profile and types of motor motion

The speed profile sets how fast the motor accelerates, decelerates and turns. This page explains the speed profile, the kinds of motion the motor can make with it, and the four kinds of stop.

#### Speed profile

##### Overview

The speed profile sets the acceleration (acc), the deceleration (dec) and the maximum speed (maxSpeed) of the motor before it moves. What values the motor can take depends on:

- the specifications of the motor
- the power supply voltage
- the load
- voltage mode or current mode

The firmware has default values, but you need to set the values for your own environment, which takes some trial and error.

##### Setting the profile

Use `/setSpeedProfile` to set the three values. Acceleration and deceleration can be set only while the motor is stopped (or HiZ). While the motor is turning, the board replies `/error/command MotorNotStopped` and keeps the old values. The maximum speed can be set at any time with `/setMaxSpeed`.

The same applies to the other settings that are written to the driver only when the motor is stopped: `/setAcc`, `/setDec`, `/setMinSpeed` and `/enableLowSpeedOptimize`, and the Raw versions of them. Which commands need which state is shown in each command as the executable timing; see also Command executable timing.

The acceleration and deceleration are rounded to the nearest value that the driver can hold, so the value that `/getSpeedProfile` returns can differ slightly from the one you set.

You can also set the minimum speed (minSpeed) with `/setMinSpeed`. It is rarely used in an actual application, but the motor turns at this speed in `/releaseSw`, the second step of the homing. If the minimum speed is below 5 steps/s, `/releaseSw` turns at 5 steps/s. While low speed optimization is enabled, the minimum speed is 0 (the register holds the threshold of the optimization instead), so `/releaseSw` turns at 5 steps/s.

#### Types of motor motion

##### Constant speed

`/run` drives the motor at a constant speed. The motor follows the acceleration and deceleration of the speed profile until it reaches the speed, and then it keeps the speed until `/run 0` or a stop command is sent. The motor does not exceed the maximum speed of the speed profile: a faster speed is limited to it. The motor is BUSY while it accelerates and decelerates.

`/goUntil` and `/releaseSw` are also constant speed commands.

##### Positioning

A positioning motion moves the motor to a target position in a trapezoidal profile. It accelerates at the configured acceleration, runs at the maximum speed once it reaches it, and decelerates at the configured deceleration, timed so that the motor stops at the target position. When the distance is short or the acceleration and deceleration are slow, the deceleration can start before the maximum speed is reached. The motor is BUSY until it stops.

`/goTo` and `/move` are typical positioning commands. `/goHome`, `/goMark` and `/goToDir` are also positioning commands.

A positioning motion in progress can be interrupted by another one, except for `/move`: `/goTo`, `/goToDir`, `/goHome` and `/goMark` are accepted while the motor is BUSY (the firmware first clears the BUSY state). `/move` is not: the driver ignores it while the motor is running, and the board then replies `/error/command CommandIgnored`.

##### Servo mode

The servo mode is not a function of the motor driver but a way of driving that the firmware implements. It keeps updating a constant speed motion so that the motor follows a target position that you give in real time, like a radio-controlled servo motor. While the motor is in this mode, the other motion commands are rejected with `InServoMode`. See Servo mode.

#### Types of stop

There are two choices, which make four commands:

- decelerate according to the speed profile, or stop instantly
- keep the motor energized, or make it HiZ (high impedance) after it stops

| State after the stop | Decelerating stop | Instant stop |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Energized | `/softStop` | `/hardStop` |
| HiZ | `/softHiZ` | `/hardHiZ` |

In voltage mode a voltage according to KVAL_HOLD is applied to an energized motor, and in current mode a current according to TVAL_HOLD flows in it, so the motor keeps its position. In the HiZ state the outputs of the driver are high impedance, no current flows in the motor, and the motor does not hold its position. **A load that the motor is carrying can fall or lose its position when the motor is HiZ.**

For a motor with an electromagnetic brake, the commands that make the motor HiZ also engage the brake, and the stop commands act differently depending on the state of the brake. See Electromagnetic brake.

#### Related commands and settings

Related commands: see the section OSC commands.

Related configuration items: see the section Configuration file.

### Homing and position management

A stepper motor does not know where it is when the board starts. This page explains why you need homing, how the HOME and LIMIT switches are used, what the homing commands do, and what to keep in mind when you manage the position.

#### Stepper motor and homing

When the system powers up, it does not know where the motor is. It could be pointing in any direction, depending on where it stopped when the system was last shut down.

If the stepper motor receives an external force that exceeds its limit, the steps slip out of alignment (**stall**). The motor then keeps working with an unknown offset between the position in the program and the physical position.

Applications that have a position or an orientation must therefore use a sensor to detect a reference position on startup, or periodically while they are running. This action is called **homing**.

After the board restarts, and after the motor has been HiZ, do homing again: the position is not reliable any more. This is especially important for a motor with an electromagnetic brake; see Electromagnetic brake.

#### Switches and sensors

Two configurations of homing sensors

Photointerrupters are often used as home sensors. On the left, a piece of white plastic attached to the slider blocks the light between the emitter and the receiver of the photointerrupter. The right side is an example of a rotary table where the photointerrupter responds to the black screw. Microswitches and photoelectric sensors are also used.

#### The HOME and LIMIT switches

Each axis of the STEP400 and the STEP800 has a HOME terminal where a sensor or a switch can be connected, with a 5 V power supply for the sensor. The STEP400 has a LIMIT terminal as well. A sensor on a terminal is called the HOME switch or the LIMIT switch. For the pin assignment and how to connect a switch or a sensor, see Sensors and switches.

##### HOME

The HOME terminal is connected directly to the motor driver and works with the homing function of the driver. It is normally used for the home sensor.

##### LIMIT (STEP400 only)

Some applications need two sensors. A slider, for example, has a limited range of motion, and if it stalls while it is moving, it can collide with one of the ends. Sensors at both ends prevent this.

The motor can be set to stop forcibly when a switch is on. The switches can also be used as simple inputs, separate from the motor operation: for example, you can connect a push button and have the board send an OSC message when it is pressed.

A switch is on when its input is LOW. The combination of the mechanism and the sensor must make the signal of the sensor go from HIGH to LOW at the home position (see Sensors and switches for the sensors and the wiring). The commands `/setHomeSwMode` and `/setLimitSwMode` set what the board does when the switch turns on.

##### Hard stop mode and `SW_USER`

The setting of the HOME switch (and the LIMIT switch on the STEP400) is either `SW_HARD_STOP` or `SW_USER`; see `/setHomeSwMode` and `/setLimitSwMode`. With `SW_HARD_STOP` the motor makes a hard stop at the moment the switch turns on. It does not look at the direction of the motion: a motor that moves away from the switch is stopped as well. Use the collision prevention settings below to restrict the direction. In the servo mode the firmware also judges the direction itself; see Servo mode.

##### Collision prevention settings

You can limit the direction in which the motor can turn while the HOME or LIMIT switch is on. With `/setProhibitMotionOnHomeSw` and `/setProhibitMotionOnLimitSw`, you can prohibit the motion toward `homingDirection` while the HOME switch is on, and the motion in the opposite direction while the LIMIT switch is on. This prevents the mechanism from running into its ends with a wrong command. A motion command that does not meet the condition is rejected with `HomeSwActivating` or `LimitSwActivating`; see the motion start condition.

For `/goTo`, `/goHome`, `/goMark` and `/goToDir` the direction of the motion is the direction of the way to the target that the driver takes (the shortest way, with wrap-around). Before v2.2.0 the board judged this direction wrongly for a target that was close, so a short move away from the switch was refused.

`homingDirection` is set with `/setHomingDirection` or with the browser configuration tool. It is also used for `/homing`.

Homing direction

#### Homing commands

The homing command is `/homing`. It combines two commands that the motor driver provides, `/goUntil` and `/releaseSw`. This section explains them first.

##### `/goUntil`

First the motor moves toward the home sensor with `/goUntil`. When the sensor turns on, the motor decelerates and stops (with `SW_HARD_STOP` of `/setHomeSwMode` it stops at once).

##### `/releaseSw`

`/releaseSw` moves the motor slowly in the opposite direction from the current position, and stops it immediately when the sensor turns off. The position where the motor stops is the home position. Strictly speaking, with `SW_USER`, `/goUntil` does not stop at the moment the sensor turns on; the motor decelerates first, so it stops a little away from the point where the sensor responded. The firmware does not correct this, because every environment is different.

With the argument `ACT`, both commands reset the current position to 0 (`ACT` 0) or copy it to the MARK register (`ACT` 1) when the sensor changes: `/goUntil` when it turns on, `/releaseSw` when it turns off. `/homing` resets it to 0.

A demonstration video of `/goUntil` and `/releaseSw`: Homing demo (Vimeo)

##### `/homing`

You can send the two commands one after the other over OSC, but `/homing` runs the whole sequence as one command. It completes the home sequence automatically in the homing direction and at the homing speed that you set beforehand with the browser configuration tool or with `/setHomingDirection` and `/setHomingSpeed`.

The progress is reported with `/homingStatus` (and `/getHomingStatus` asks for it). The homing ends with `HOMING_COMPLETED` when `/releaseSw` has finished, or with `HOMING_TIMEOUT` when a timeout elapsed (below). The values are listed at `/homingStatus`. A motion command that you send during the homing clears the homing state.

`/goUntil`, `/goUntilRaw` and `/releaseSw` are rejected with `InServoMode` while the motor is in the servo mode, and `/homing` is rejected with `BrakeEngaged` while the brake of the motor is not released.

##### Homing timeouts

Both `/goUntil` and `/releaseSw` have timeouts, set with `/setGoUntilTimeout` and `/setReleaseSwTimeout`. When the state of the sensor has not changed within the time, the board stops the motor with a hard stop and sends `/error/command GoUntilTimeout` or `ReleaseSwTimeout`. This prevents the moving part from being pushed against a mechanical end forever when the sensor does not respond.

##### Homing at startup

When `driverSettings.homingAtStartup` is set, the board starts the homing after it starts. For a motor with an electromagnetic brake, the board releases the brake first and starts the homing when the brake is released.

#### Rotary tables

When the home sensor responds to a hole or to a part that has a width, the position at which the sensor responds differs between clockwise and counterclockwise rotation by that width. The board can notify both the change from HIGH to LOW and the change from LOW to HIGH of the home sensor with an OSC message. The message also contains the direction of the rotation, so you can align the home position if you write a sequence for each direction. Enable this notification with `/enableHomeSwReport`.

#### Position management

- `/setPosition` and `/resetPos` change the position that the board holds. **Do not send them while the motor is in the servo mode or moving.** The board does not guard against this; the motor can behave unexpectedly.
- `/setMark` stores a position that `/goMark` goes to.
- When the microstep setting changes, the coordinate system changes too; see Voltage mode and current mode.

#### Related commands and settings

Related commands: see the section OSC commands.

Related configuration items: see the section Configuration file.

### Servo mode

The servo mode lets the motor follow a target position that changes in real time. This page explains what the mode is, how to start it and how to give the target, and how to tune the PID gains.

#### What the servo mode is

The servo mode is not a function of the motor driver IC. Positioning commands of the driver need the target position to be set before the motion starts. In the servo mode, you can define a new target position *while the motor is moving*, like a radio-controlled servo motor. While the mode is active, the other motion commands cannot be sent: they are rejected with `InServoMode`.

The control of the servo mode

The firmware updates the speed of the motor every 5 ms. At each update it compares the current position with the target, calculates the speed with the PID control described below, and sends it to the driver as a constant speed command. (Until v2.1.0 the period was 10 ms.) The integral and derivative terms are scaled by the period, so the same gains were designed to give about the same response as before; the response can still differ a little, and you may need to tune the gains again.

#### Starting the servo mode

##### Toggling the mode

`/enableServoMode` starts and stops the servo mode. When the mode starts, the board stops the motor with a hard stop, makes the current position the target position, and clears the integral and the previous error of the PID control. For a motor with an electromagnetic brake, `/enableServoMode 1` is a motion command: while the brake is engaged, the board replies `BrakeEngaged` and does not start the mode (see the motion start condition).

When the mode stops, the board stops the motor with a soft stop and keeps it energized. For a motor with an electromagnetic brake, what `/enableServoMode 0` does depends on the state of the brake; see Electromagnetic brake.

**Notifications are turned off.** When the servo mode starts, the notifications of `/busy`, `/motorStatus` and `/dir` are disabled (the settings that `/enableBusyReport`, `/enableMotorStatusReport` and `/enableDirReport` make). They are not enabled again when the mode stops. Enable them again if you need them.

##### Updating the target position

`/setTargetPosition` updates the target position. When the firmware receives a new target, it compares it with the current position and changes the speed of the motor. `/setTargetPositionList` sends the targets of all the motors at once.

##### Cases where the servo mode stops or is not available

- `/goUntil`, `/goUntilRaw` and `/releaseSw` reply `InServoMode` and do nothing while the motor is in the servo mode, as the other motion commands and `/homing` do.
- **Do not send `/setPosition` or `/resetPos` while the motor is in the servo mode.** The board does not guard against this.
- When the driver makes the motor HiZ by itself (overcurrent, overtemperature or UVLO), the servo mode is cancelled and `ServoModeCancelledOnHiZ` is sent. The commands that make the motor HiZ cancel the servo mode first. To resume, send `/enableServoMode 1` again; the current position becomes the target. See Alarms and protection.
- **In the servo mode, the firmware watches the switches itself** (in addition to the driver). At every update, it sets the speed to 0 if the motor would move in a prohibited direction: toward `homingDirection` while the HOME switch is on, and (STEP400 only) away from `homingDirection` while the LIMIT switch is on. This applies to a switch whose motion is prohibited (`/setProhibitMotionOnHomeSw`, `/setProhibitMotionOnLimitSw`) or whose mode is the hard stop mode. The two switches are judged separately, so a pressed HOME switch does not hide the LIMIT switch. Motion in the other direction is not blocked, so the motor can move away from a switch. The STEP800 has the HOME switch only. When the HOME switch turns on in the hard stop mode, the motor also makes a hard stop at once, whichever direction it moves (see Hard stop mode and `SW_USER`).

#### Control parameters

The speed of the motor is calculated with a technique called PID control. `/setServoParam` sets the three gains of it.

##### Proportional gain (kP)

PID control uses the difference between the current position and the target position (the deviation). The motor turns faster when the deviation is large and slower when it is small, so it approaches the target. The proportional gain sets how much the deviation influences the speed. If it is too small, the approach takes a long time; if it is too large, the motor overshoots the target.

##### Integral gain (kI)

With the proportional control only, the motor gets slower as it approaches the target, and it takes a very long time to remove the last small deviation. Adding the time integral of the deviation to the control value removes it. A large integral gain removes the deviation quickly, but it can cause overshoot, and the motion that compensates for the overshoot can cause continuous oscillation.

##### Derivative gain (kD)

When the motor overshoots or oscillates, this gain works against the steep changes of the deviation. It acts like a damper that reduces each oscillation.

#### Determining the PID parameters

##### Step by step

The PID gains depend on the acceleration, the deceleration and the maximum speed that the motor can actually use (the speed profile). Determine them in this order:

1. Decide the KVAL (the TVAL in current mode) that suits the rating of the motor and the load. See Voltage mode and current mode.
2. Decide the acceleration, the deceleration and the maximum speed that the motor can use. See Speed profile and types of motor motion.
3. Adjust the PID gains.

##### Deciding the gains

There are many methods to decide the best gains. They depend on the purpose of the motion and on how often the target changes. We recommend this approach, with trial and error on the real setup.

###### 1. kP

Set kP, kI and kD to 0.0, and raise kP gradually until the motor starts to oscillate around its target. When the target changes only from time to time, we often set only kP and keep kI and kD at 0.0.

###### 2. kI

When the target changes only once every few seconds, a higher kI makes the motion more agile. When the target is sent at 60 fps, however, the acceleration toward each new target can cause vibration and spoil the smoothness. The value depends on whether a quick response to the target or a smooth overall motion is more important.

###### 3. kD

Raise kD gradually if you see oscillation or overshoot when the motor approaches the target.

#### Related commands and settings

Related commands: see the section OSC commands.

Related configuration items: see the section Configuration file.

### Electromagnetic brake

An electromagnetic brake locks the shaft of the motor when it is not powered. This page explains how the board controls the brake together with the motor: the states of the brake, what each command does to it, and what you must know before you hang a load on the motor.

#### What an electromagnetic brake is

Some stepper motors have an electromagnetic brake built in. A stepper motor keeps a holding torque while it is stopped and energized. If the power is lost, the torque is lost, and a suspended load moves or falls. The brake locks the shaft when its power is off (or when you command it) and releases the shaft when it is powered. It is needed especially when a load is moved up and down.

The board controls the brake output of each motor on its own. It supports the STEP400 with the EMB-STEP400 brake board and the brake outputs of the STEP800. For the wiring, see Electromagnetic brake wiring. For the specifications of the brake board, see EMB-STEP400.

#### Enabling the brake

Enable the brake of a motor with `/enableElectromagnetBrake` or with `driverSettings.electromagnetBrakeEnable` in the configuration. While the brake is enabled, the board releases the brake when the motor is energized and engages it when the motor is not energized, by itself. The brake behavior on this page does not apply to a motor whose brake is not enabled (the last paragraph of Stopping a motor that is going to engage the brake is the one exception).

The setting can be changed only while the driver is HiZ and, to disable the brake, only while it is engaged or after `/free`; otherwise the board replies `CommandIgnored`.

#### States of the brake

The brake of each motor is in one of six states. `/getBrakeStatus` returns the number. The numbers are part of the specification; new states will only be added as 6, 7, ... A motor whose brake is disabled has the state -1.

| State | Name | Brake output | Driver | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 0 | Engaged | engaged | HiZ | The brake holds the shaft. The motor is not energized. |
| 1 | Releasing | engaged | energized | `/activate 1` was sent. The board waits for the transition duration, then releases the brake. |
| 2 | Released | released | energized | The motor is energized and the shaft is free. Motion commands are accepted. |
| 3 | Stopping | released | energized | `/softHiZ` or `/activate 0` is decelerating the motor. When the motor has stopped, the brake is engaged. |
| 4 | Engaging | engaged | energized | The brake is engaged and the motor is still energized. After the transition duration the driver goes HiZ. |
| 5 | Free | released | HiZ | `/free` was sent. The brake is released and the motor is not energized. |

##### How the state changes

Besides the commands (see below), the board changes the state by itself. It reads the state of the driver every 5 ms and decides at that moment:

| From | When | To |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Releasing | the driver is energized and the transition duration has passed | Released (the brake output is released) |
| Releasing | the driver is HiZ (for example the motor has no power) | Engaged, and `/error/command BrakeReleaseFailed` |
| Stopping | the motor has stopped | Engaging |
| Engaging | the transition duration has passed, or the driver is found HiZ | Engaged (the driver is made HiZ in the first case) |
| Released, Stopping | the driver went HiZ by itself (overcurrent, overtemperature, UVLO) | Engaged at once, and `/error/command BrakeEngagedOnHiZ`. Pending motions are cancelled. |

Because the state is read every 5 ms, a transition happens up to 5 ms after the command.

#### Commands and the brake

This is what each command does to a motor with the brake enabled. "Nothing" means that the command is not executed and no error is sent.

| Command | Engaged (0) | Releasing (1) | Released (2) | Stopping (3) | Engaging (4) | Free (5) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `/activate 1` | energizes the driver, then Releasing | nothing | nothing | cancels the engaging, Released; the deceleration goes on | back to Releasing (the wait starts again) | energizes the driver, Released |
| `/activate 0`, `/softHiZ` | nothing | Engaging | decelerates the motor, Stopping | nothing | nothing | Engaged |
| `/hardHiZ` | nothing | Engaging | stops the motor at once, Engaging | stops the motor at once, Engaging | nothing | Engaged |
| `/free` | HiZ with the brake released, Free | same | same | same | same | nothing |
| Motion commands (`/run`, `/move`, `/goTo`, ..., `/homing`, `/enableServoMode 1`) | `BrakeEngaged` | `BrakeEngaged` | executed | executed, Released (the engaging is cancelled) | `BrakeEngaged` | executed, the motor is energized, Released |
| `/softStop`, `/hardStop`, `/enableServoMode 0` | nothing | executed | executed | executed, Released (the engaging is cancelled) | executed | nothing |
| `/resetMotorDriver` | executed | `CommandIgnored` | `CommandIgnored` | `CommandIgnored` | `CommandIgnored` | executed |

A motion command while the brake is engaged is rejected with `BrakeEngaged`; this is part of the motion start condition.

The commands for all motors (255) and the combined commands (`/combine/...`) act on each motor like this.

##### Stopping a motor that is going to engage the brake

While the motor decelerates after `/softHiZ` or `/activate 0` (state Stopping), **the command that arrived last wins**:

- `/softStop`, `/hardStop` and `/enableServoMode 0` cancel the plan to engage the brake. The state returns to Released and the motor stops and stays energized. These commands mean "stop and hold", so they override the earlier "stop and engage the brake". If you want the brake after that, send `/softHiZ`, `/activate 0` or `/hardHiZ` again.
- `/hardHiZ` does not cancel the plan: it stops the motor at once and engages the brake.
- `/softHiZ` and `/activate 0` do nothing: the deceleration and the plan go on.
- A motion command and `/activate 1` also cancel the plan; the brake stays released.

The same happens for a motor whose brake is not enabled: a `/softStop` sent during the deceleration of a `/softHiZ` leaves the motor energized.

#### Transition duration

The brake needs a short time to work mechanically, so the motor and the brake must hold the shaft together for a while. The **transition duration** (`/setBrakeTransitionDuration`, `driverSettings.brakeTransitionDuration`) is this overlap:

- To release: the board energizes the motor, waits for the transition duration, then releases the brake.
- To engage: the board engages the brake, waits for the transition duration, then makes the motor HiZ.

Brake transition duration

The duration does not change how long the brake takes to lock; it changes how long the board waits before it makes the motor HiZ or releases the brake. The wait is counted in 5 ms steps, so the actual time is 0 to 5 ms longer than the setting.

We do not give a recommended value: it depends on the response time of your brake, on the load and on the device. Set a value that is the release and engage time in the specification of the brake plus a margin. See `/setBrakeTransitionDuration` for the initial value and the range.

#### Holding current

When a motor with the brake enabled is energized again (`/activate 1`, and a motion command after `/free`), KVAL_HOLD (TVAL_HOLD in current mode) is raised to at least half of KVAL_RUN (TVAL_RUN), so that the motor holds the load while the brake is released. `/getKval` returns the raised value. See Voltage mode and current mode.

#### Restart, watchdog and CPU fault

The board engages the brakes before it restarts, whatever the reason:

- **`/resetDevice` and the `R` command of the USB serial port**: the board stops the motors that are turning with a hard stop, engages their brakes, waits for the longest transition duration of them (at most 1 s), and then restarts.
- **Watchdog**: when the processing stops for about 250 ms, the board engages every brake, waits for the longest transition duration (at most 1 s), and then the watchdog restarts the board. Nothing is sent to the drivers; a turning motor is stopped by the brake. `/booted` reports the reset cause 4.
- **CPU fault** (an exception of the CPU): the board engages every brake at once, waits in the same way, and restarts. `/booted` reports the reset cause 6.

The reset cause is the second argument of `/booted`; see there for the numbers.

When the USB cable is pulled out while the Ethernet cable is connected, the STEP400 (R1 board) can restart (a hardware problem). The brakes are engaged first, but pull the cable out only while the motors are stopped.

#### When the load is not held

The firmware cannot prevent these times in which the load is not held:

- **Power-on of the STEP800**: all the brakes stay released for about 250 ms after the power is applied, mostly the time of the bootloader. **Depending on the power supply and the conditions, it can be longer: with 24 V, the brakes stayed released for about 2 s in a measurement.** This depends on the hardware, not on the firmware.
- **The RESET switch and a drop of the supply voltage**: the drivers are in standby and the brakes (STEP800) stay released for about 0.5 s, until the firmware starts.
- On the STEP400 with the EMB-STEP400, the brakes engage at once also at a reset (the brake board pulls them down).
- Even when the brake is engaged electrically first, the shaft is held only after the brake has locked mechanically, which takes tens of ms.

If you hang a load on the motor, take these times into account.

#### Usage notes

- **Take the power of the brake from the same power supply as the motor, or from a supply that is cut together with the power of the motor.** Do not let only the power of the motor be cut first: the holding force is then lost before the undervoltage lockout acts, and the load falls. The brake and the motor can use different voltages (for example, a 48 V motor and a 24 V brake); in that case, make the brake supply follow the motor supply.
- **Do homing again after a restart, and after the motor has been HiZ.** The position is not reliable: after the motor is energized again, the first release of the brake can shift the shaft. See Homing and position management.
- **`/free` is for maintenance.** It releases the motor and keeps the brake released, so a load that hangs on the motor falls. Be very careful with this command; make the load safe before you send it.
- The motor turns only when the brake is released: see the motion start condition above.
- For the driver that goes HiZ by itself, the board engages the brake (`BrakeEngagedOnHiZ`); see Alarms and protection.

Stepper motor with brake

PKP243D23M2

### Alarms and protection

The driver ICs detect four kinds of alarms: a drop of the supply voltage (UVLO), overtemperature, overcurrent and stall. This page explains what each alarm means, what the driver does, and what the board sends to you.

#### Overview

Each alarm has a flag in the status of the driver. The board reads the status of every driver every 5 ms, and sends a message when the status changes (see Timing of the notifications). Whether a message is sent is set for each alarm with an `/enable...Report` command. The alarms differ in what the driver does:

| Alarm | What the driver does | Message |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Undervoltage lockout (UVLO) | turns off the outputs: the motor is HiZ | `/uvlo` |
| Overtemperature | warning: nothing. Bridge shutdown or device shutdown: the motor is HiZ | `/thermalStatus` |
| Overcurrent | turns off the outputs: the motor is HiZ | `/overCurrent` |
| Stall | nothing (only a flag) | `/stall` |

The PowerSTEP01 of the STEP400 and the L6470 of the STEP800 differ in the details. This page notes where they do.

#### The alarms

##### UVLO: undervoltage lockout

UVLO happens when the supply voltage of the driver falls below the turn-off threshold. The driver turns off all the outputs at once, so the motor is HiZ and cannot be operated while the condition lasts. The condition ends when the voltage is above the turn-on threshold; then see Resuming. The thresholds are different on the STEP400 and on the STEP800; see the datasheets of the driver ICs.

`/enableUvloReport` turns the notification on (the message `/uvlo` is sent when the state changes). `/getUvlo` reads the state.

##### Overtemperature

The driver monitors its temperature. At the warning level, only a flag is set and the operation is not limited. At the shutdown level the outputs are turned off, so the motor is HiZ. The STEP400 has two shutdown levels (bridge shutdown and device shutdown); the STEP800 has one. The temperatures are listed at `/thermalStatus`.

`/enableThermalStatusReport` turns the notification on, and `/getThermalStatus` reads the state. The motor is HiZ with or without the notification. After a shutdown, see Resuming.

##### Overcurrent

The driver measures the current of the power transistors. When the current exceeds the threshold, the driver turns off the outputs (the firmware keeps this protection on), so the motor is HiZ. The protection is a critical one; it is not meant to be turned off.

`/setOverCurrentThreshold` sets the threshold, `/enableOverCurrentReport` turns the notification on, and then `/overCurrent` is sent when an overcurrent occurs. To start the motor again after the cause has gone, see Resuming (a motor with the electromagnetic brake needs `/activate 1` first).

##### Stall

The stall detection lets the driver find out, from the current of the motor, that the motor can no longer turn against the load. The driver only sets a flag; it does not stop the motor. The detection works only in voltage mode on the STEP400: it is not available in current mode.

`/setStallThreshold` sets the threshold and `/enableStallReport` turns the notification on. See Using the stall detection.

#### Timing of the notifications

- The board reads the state of the drivers every 5 ms. The messages `/busy`, `/HiZ`, `/uvlo`, `/thermalStatus` and so on are sent when the state changes, not at every read.
- `/overCurrent` and `/stall` are sent at once when the condition starts. While it lasts, they are sent at most every 200 ms for each motor and each kind. A detection within the 200 ms is not lost; it gives one message at the end of the interval. A detection while the notification is disabled is not sent later.
- `/getStatus` and `/getStatusList` read the status of the driver without clearing the latched flags (OCD, stall, UVLO, SW_EVN and so on). Only the poll of the board every 5 ms clears them, so a `/getStatus` or `/getStatusList` sent right after another one can show a flag that the earlier reply showed (until the next poll, up to 5 ms).

#### When the driver goes HiZ by itself

When the driver makes the motor HiZ because of an overcurrent shutdown, an overtemperature shutdown or UVLO, the board does the following, in this order (each message follows its own setting):

1. `/HiZ` (when `/enableHizReport` is on).
2. If the motor is in the servo mode: the servo mode is cancelled and `/error/command ServoModeCancelledOnHiZ` is sent. Nothing is sent to the driver.
3. If the motor has an electromagnetic brake that is released: the brake is engaged at the next status read (up to 5 ms later) and `/error/command BrakeEngagedOnHiZ` is sent. See Electromagnetic brake.

The errors follow `/reportError`. The commands that make a motor HiZ (`/softHiZ`, `/hardHiZ`, `/activate 0`, `/free`, `/resetMotorDriver`) cancel the servo mode first and do not send `ServoModeCancelledOnHiZ`.

##### Resuming

After the cause (the overcurrent, the temperature or the supply voltage) is gone, the motor is still HiZ. Start it again with a motion command. A motor with the electromagnetic brake enabled needs `/activate 1` first, because the board has engaged its brake (a motion command is rejected with `BrakeEngaged` while the brake is engaged). To resume the servo mode, send `/enableServoMode 1` (after `/activate 1` for a motor with the brake); the current position becomes the target. If the cause remains, the driver shuts down again.

#### Thresholds and currents

The thresholds of the overcurrent and of the stall are set with a number, and the current of a number is

> current = (value + 1) × step

The step depends on the driver:

| | Overcurrent | Stall |
| --- | --- | --- |
| STEP400 (PowerSTEP01) | 312.5 mA | 312.5 mA |
| STEP800 (L6470) | 375 mA | 31.25 mA |

The value 0 is one step, not 0 A. The datasheet of the PowerSTEP01 gives these thresholds as voltages (31.25 mV steps for the stall); the conversion to the current is the one of the sensing circuit of the STEP400. The same kind of conversion applies to TVAL in current mode, with a step of 78.125 mA (Voltage mode and current mode). The ranges and the initial values depend on the board, so they are written only in `/setOverCurrentThreshold` and `/setStallThreshold`.

#### Using the stall detection

The stall detection compares the current of the motor with a threshold. Find the threshold by trial: it should be as close as possible to the current that actually flows, and a little above it. A small loss of steps cannot be detected, but a large position error may be detected.

The current depends on KVAL and on the back-EMF compensation, so adjust them to the motor and to the supply voltage first: see Voltage mode and current mode.

#### Switches that prohibit a motion

The motion that the HOME and LIMIT switches prohibit (`/setProhibitMotionOnHomeSw`, `/setProhibitMotionOnLimitSw`) is described in Homing and position management.
